abstract: Gene transcription regulatory networks let cells encode an internal representation of their environment as patterns of protein expression. Among the thirteen connected directed subgraphs on three nodes, the feed-forward loop (FFL) is the one consistently over-represented in transcriptional networks relative to randomizations that preserve the node degrees, yet its eight structural variants occur very unequally: in Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cerevisiae the C1 and I1 variants dominate and the other six are rare. We ask whether the trade-off between cost and information in these architectures can rationalize this asymmetry. Each variant is treated as a noisy channel from the environment to the output expression level, with a channel capacity obtained from the Lyapunov equation of the linearized chemical Langevin dynamics and a protein burden from the mean of the regulated proteins at steady state. The analytical capacity agrees with mutual information estimated from Gillespie simulations across families, gates, and Hill coefficients. We compare the eight variants on the Pareto frontier of the cost-information plane under four information measures and ten promoter logics. Two results follow. First, only C1, C3, I1, and I3 are ever Pareto winners within their family, while C2, C4, I2, and I4 never win, consistent with their rarity; C1 robustly dominates the coherent family, in agreement with the census. Second, no measure separates I1 from I3 by more than a few percentage points, and the measures disagree on which is ahead, so cost and information treat the two as nearly equivalent. In the census, by contrast, I1 outnumbers I3 by 21:1 in S. cerevisiae. Cost and information thus account for the exclusion of four variants and for the dominance of C1, but not for the dominance of I1, whose separation from I3 may require a measure of response timing, which our measures of the environmental level do not probe.
